cards.title: Start with free cash flow, not net income, to judge business health
cards.summary: Net income can be positive while the bank balance falls; free cash flow (operating cash flow minus investing cash flow) reveals whether the business actually funded itself.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly financial review of an ecommerce store, when net income looks healthy but the cash balance is shrinking or we are unsure whether to hire, buy inventory or take on debt.
steps: Compute free cash flow as operating cash flow minus investing cash flow, and compare it to net income side by side for each period. The source's case study shows six months where net income was positive every month but free cash flow was positive in only two of those months.
Treat the deeper definition as the operating question: after funding 100% of internal operations and necessary asset investments, is there any cash left over?

Identify which line item caused the gap in each period — in the case study the two big swing factors were lumpy inventory purchases and capitalised software development spending, not the profit and loss statement.

Because leftover free cash flow is the pool available for debt repayment, owner distributions or reinvestment, use it (not net income) to decide whether the store can afford a new hire, a bigger inventory buy or a loan payment.

Use net cash flow (after financing) for a holistic view of whether the business can service debt and run itself at the same time; the source notes it is lower than free cash flow whenever the business carries leverage.
caveats: The three-statement logic applies to all business models, but the specific swing factors differ — for ecommerce, inventory and capitalised development dominated.
Depreciation, debt principal repayments and capitalised software are invisible on the income statement, so a P&L-only review will systematically miss cash drains.

cards.title: Map the three cash flow statement sections to store activities
cards.summary: Operating, investing and financing sections each capture different cash movements, and knowing which section an ecommerce transaction belongs to prevents misreading cash health.
cards.use_when: When setting up or reviewing an ecommerce cash flow statement and deciding where to record inventory buys, software build costs, loan drawdowns or owner distributions.
steps: Operating cash flow (also called cash flow from operations): everything related to running day-to-day operations — paying salaries, marketing, fulfilment and supplier bills. Start this section with net income linked from the income statement, then adjust.

Investing cash flow: purchases of long-term assets such as warehouse equipment, a software platform, or shares in another company. A one-month employee salary is an expense (operating), not an investment.
Financing cash flow: non-operational capital movements — owner distributions, money lent into the business, loan proceeds or repayments. This reflects capital structure, not trading performance.

Adjust operating cash flow for balance sheet movements: a rise in accounts receivable is negative to cash (customers owe you), a rise in accounts payable is positive (you owe suppliers and hold cash longer), and depreciation is stripped back out because it never left the bank.
Apply the same treatment to inventory: an increase in the inventory balance (e.g. 335k to 448k) is a cash outflow, and a decrease means you converted stock into sales and released cash.
Only after completing all three sections do you arrive at free cash flow, which the source describes as cash with no further obligations other than financing.
caveats: The exact interface and line-item naming varies by accounting software and template; verify current layouts when building or importing statements.
The source teaches the general structure via one ecommerce example, so line items specific to your store may need judgement.

cards.title: Why inventory purchases make a profitable store run out of cash
cards.summary: Buying stock in large lumps hits cash in the purchase month while the cost only reaches the P&L when goods sell, so profitable periods can coincide with cash shortages.
cards.use_when: Planning inventory replenishment or a seasonal stock buy for an ecommerce store, or explaining why a high-revenue month did not improve the bank balance.
steps: Recognise that product costs on the income statement do not match cash out: you manufacture or buy in large batches, capitalise them on the balance sheet, warehouse them, then sell through over later months.
Track the change in the inventory balance each period rather than only cost of goods sold. When inventory rose 113k in the case study month, that amount was cash out of the business.

Expect the opposite in sell-through months: when inventory falls, the business converts stock directly into sales and releases cash, which is why free cash flow can exceed net income (e.g. net income 140 vs free cash flow 272 in the case study month).
Before committing to a large buy, model the month the cash leaves versus the months the sales land, and confirm the store can absorb the dip even if the P&L still shows a profit.

Note the compounding effect on margin: in the case study month where orders more than doubled on a promotion, gross margin percentage fell because the volume was sold at a discount, so a cash-heavy buy funded a lower-margin sell-through.
caveats: The case study numbers are illustrative of one store's model, not benchmarks for expected inventory turns or margin levels.
Inventory dynamics will differ by model — made-to-order, dropship or pre-order stores carry very different cash timing.

cards.title: Discount-driven revenue spikes lower gross margin percentage
cards.summary: In the case study, the month where orders more than doubled during a sale also saw gross margin percentage drop, so monitor margin percentage alongside revenue volume.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a sitewide sale, promotion or discount event, and evaluating the margin consequence after the event.
steps: Track gross margin as a percentage of revenue every period, not just gross profit in absolute terms. In the case study the percentage is relatively stable until the promotional month.

Expect a promotional month to increase order volume while lowering margin percentage, because products are sold at a discount — in the case study orders roughly doubled in the sale month and margin percentage declined.
After the sale, watch whether margin percentage recovers to the pre-sale baseline, as it does in the following months of the case study.

Combine this with the cash view: a sale that lifts volume but is paired with a large inventory build can still consume cash, so evaluate the promotion on margin percentage, free cash flow and inventory movement together.

Use the sale-month pattern to plan cash: if you discount to move stock, you may release inventory cash even as margin percentage falls, which the case study shows as a free cash flow higher than net income in the sell-through month.
caveats: The case study does not establish a target margin band or a discount depth that is safe; treat its figures as an illustration of the relationship rather than a rule.
A margin drop may be acceptable for strategic reasons (clearing stock, acquiring customers) that a P&L percentage alone will not capture.

cards.title: Capitalised software development hides cash outflow from the P&L
cards.summary: Capitalising developer payroll pushes cost to the balance sheet and spreads it over its useful life, so the P&L shows a fraction of the actual cash being spent.
cards.use_when: Budgeting for building or extending a custom storefront, app or platform with an in-house or contracted engineering team, and reviewing why cash is leaving faster than reported expenses suggest.
steps: Understand the mechanics: instead of expensing an engineering payroll of 100k in month one, the cost is capitalised and spread over the useful life — the source notes software is typically amortised over about 36 months.

Track the balance of capitalised software assets and the change each period. In the case study the store spent 240k on its software platform across six months while only 40k showed up as depreciation expense.
Treat each increase in the capitalised software balance as an investing cash outflow, since the money genuinely left the business even though it does not hit the P&L that month.

When reviewing reported profitability, add back the cash actually spent on the platform to see the true funding requirement; the source identifies this as one of the two main reasons a net-income-positive month had a deeply negative free cash flow (-95k).

When planning cash, fund the full development spend rather than the amortised portion, and remember that the remaining amortisation will keep hitting the P&L for up to three years even if the project stops.
caveats: Amortisation periods vary (the source says usually three, sometimes five years depending on what is purchased), so use your own accounting policy rather than the illustrative 36 months.
Capitalisation rules and thresholds differ by jurisdiction and accountant guidance — confirm treatment with your accountant.

cards.title: Quarterly tax payments create lumpy cash outflows, not monthly ones
cards.summary: The income statement reports an estimated tax figure each month, but most businesses actually pay in quarterly instalments, so tax cash leaves in spikes.
cards.use_when: Forecasting store cash needs around quarter-end and reconciling monthly reported profit with actual cash movement in the bank.
steps: Separate the monthly tax expense on the P&L from the actual cash payment schedule. In the case study the P&L shows a tax figure each month (e.g. 25) while the balance sheet shows the liability building up.
Watch the tax liability balance: it accumulates across the quarter, then resets when the payment is made. In the case study the store paid roughly 80k at one quarter-end and about 100k at the next.
In months with no tax payment, treat the retained amount as positive cash flow, which is one reason a free cash flow figure can exceed net income.
In the payment month, budget the lump sum as a material outflow rather than the small monthly P&L figure, and avoid committing that cash to inventory or ad spend before the quarter closes.

Remember that in the case study month with no tax payment, this was one of the factors (alongside inventory sell-through and low engineering spend) that produced free cash flow of 272 against net income of 140.
caveats: Payment frequency and estimation rules vary by country and entity type; verify your own tax calendar rather than assuming quarterly.
The case study amounts are illustrative and should not be used as expected tax rates.

cards.title: Debt principal repayments never appear on the income statement
cards.summary: Only interest on debt hits the P&L; principal repayments show up on the balance sheet and financing section, so loan drawdowns and repayments distort cash without changing reported profit.
cards.use_when: Managing a store line of credit, merchant cash advance or term loan, and judging whether reported profitability reflects the real cash burden of debt.
steps: On the income statement, look for the interest line: it confirms there is debt but shows nothing about principal movements, since debt repayments do not appear in the P&L.
On the balance sheet, track the movement in the debt or line of credit balance. In the case study the line of credit is being paid down by about 25,000 per month.
Record principal reductions in the financing section of the cash flow statement, where money coming into or out of the business for non-operational purposes belongs.

When assessing store health, use net cash flow (after financing) rather than free cash flow to answer whether the business can pay its debts and run itself at the same time — the source notes net cash flow is lower than free cash flow whenever the business has leverage.
When deciding whether to draw more on a credit line for inventory or marketing, model the impact of the additional principal repayments on future months, not just the interest expense.
caveats: The source states net cash flow relates to debt service and is therefore a less operational measure than free cash flow; do not use it alone to evaluate trading performance.
Financing structures differ (revolvers, term loans, merchant advances); map the actual repayment schedule of your facility before modelling.

cards.title: Reconcile a profitable month against a negative free cash flow month
cards.summary: Working through the case study month by month shows how to attribute a cash shortfall to specific balance sheet movements rather than to profitability.
cards.use_when: After a month where the store reported a profit but the bank balance dropped, to identify the exact causes before deciding on corrective action.
steps: Start the operating section with that month's net income and then adjust for each balance sheet change: receivables up is negative to cash, payables up is positive, depreciation is added back, and inventory increases are subtracted.
In the case study month with net income of 77k and free cash flow of -95k, the main driver was a very large inventory purchase, compounded by payments to software engineers building the platform.

In the contrasting month with net income of 140 and free cash flow of 272, the opposite dynamic applied: the store sold through a lot of inventory without buying more, paid little to the engineering team, and made no tax payment, so cash accumulated on the balance sheet.
Rank the causes by size for the month in question — inventory movement, capitalised development spend, tax timing and debt repayments are the recurring candidates in an ecommerce model.

Convert the finding into an operational decision: if the shortfall was an intentional inventory build, confirm the sell-through timeline and cash runway; if it was unplanned, address the specific driver before repeating the spend.
caveats: The case study's figures illustrate method, not your expected outcomes; apply the adjustment logic to your own numbers.
A single-month reconciliation can be distorted by seasonal or one-off items, so examine several consecutive periods before concluding.

cards.title: Separate near-cash expenses from non-cash items when reading the P&L
cards.summary: Most operating expense lines equal their cash outlay, but depreciation and product cost do not, so identify which expenses reflect money actually leaving the bank.
cards.use_when: Reviewing the store's operating expense structure to decide where cash can realistically be cut versus where cuts only change reported profit.
steps: Walk each operating expense line and classify it: personnel, ad spend, marketing consultants, insurance, office rent, software and miscellaneous generally have a cash outlay equal to the reported amount, as the source notes for a 96k monthly personnel cost.

Flag depreciation as non-cash: you purchase assets and then spread the cost, usually over three or sometimes five years depending on what is purchased, so the P&L figure does not show how much cash went out.
Flag cost of goods sold as non-cash in timing terms: you are not buying products as you sell them, you are buying in large chunks and warehousing them.
When you need to cut cash quickly, target the lines where cash outlay equals expense (payroll, marketing, rent), since cutting depreciation does not release cash.

Rebuild the true monthly outflow from the cash flow statement rather than the P&L before making spending decisions, and check whether depreciation is increasing over time, which signals the business is buying assets.
caveats: Some expenses may be prepaid or accrued, so the reported amount may not equal cash in the period even for nominally cash expenses.
The source presents this as a general structure; the classification of any specific line depends on your accounting treatment.

cards.title: Track the three statements together to see what the P&L omits
cards.summary: The income statement captures unit economics, the balance sheet reveals asset, debt and inventory movements, and the cash flow statement ties them into actual cash change.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing the store's monthly reporting pack, or when a single statement gives a misleading picture of ecommerce health.
steps: Use the income statement to judge roughly whether the unit economics say the business should make money — the source describes net income as answering that question, not the cash question.

Move to the balance sheet to see what the P&L hides: inventory balances, capitalised software, tax liability build-up and loan balances. Assets should always equal liabilities plus equity as a basic check.

Read the cash flow statement to convert those balance sheet movements into cash impacts, since it is where inventory swings, capitalised development spend, tax payments and loan repayments become visible.

Use the case study's opening contradiction as a diagnostic template: a store profitable on the P&L but losing cash is usually moving inventory, capitalising development, paying down debt or timing tax — not mis-stating revenue.

Because the concept applies to all business models, apply the same three-statement read to subscriptions, marketplaces or retail, adjusting for which balance sheet items dominate (e.g. deferred revenue for subscriptions, inventory for retail).
caveats: The source assumes familiarity with the three-statement model and links a template; if you cannot build one, the reconciliation logic is harder to apply directly.
The case study deliberately uses an ecommerce business because it exhibits nearly every dimension of cash complexity — other models omit some of these drivers.

input.text: hey everyone Eric here in this video I'm going to turn you into an expert in understanding free cash flow for startups through a finance case study the reason I created this video is because net income is often very misleading when it comes to understanding the health of a startup and free cash flow almost always clarifies what's really going on okay let's get started okay so in today's lesson we're going to analyze a three-statement financial model about an e-commerce business to understand what free cash flow is and why it's so essential to monitor it so the concept that
